sections.html:
Down in Virginia's southeastern corner, Norfolk occupies the spot where the Elizabeth River empties toward the Chesapeake Bay. No county sits over it, because Norfolk is an independent city that runs its own assessments, tax billing and zoning. Population was 238,005 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 231,013.

Of the city's 96.41 square miles, 53.28 are land and 43.13 are water. Average elevation is about 6.9 feet. Those two facts explain why buyers here ask about flooding before almost anything else.

Dozens of named neighborhoods make up the city, and a house on one street can have little in common with a house two miles away.

  • Freemason and West Freemason: historic downtown blocks holding some of Norfolk's oldest buildings.
  • Berkley: once a separate city, annexed in 1906, across the Elizabeth River.
  • Willoughby Spit and Ocean View: bay-front areas.
  • Colonial Place, Larchmont, North Shore, Edgewater and Lafayette Shores: popular residential pockets.
  • Downtown, Ghent and Fairmount Park: parts of town reshaped by revitalization.

A pre-war rowhouse in Ghent, a bayside house in Ocean View and a mid-century home in Larchmont each raise different repair and flood questions. A fast sale usually begins with a walk-through of the house, not a formula.

sections.h2: Flood zones and the Forerunner tool
sections.html:
The city is low, mostly ringed by water and slowly sinking, and some areas already flood at high tide. Tropical storm risk is highest from mid-August through September, when heavy rain and wind can hit.

Zones come from FEMA's Flood Insurance Rate Map. Norfolk applies them through Article 3.9.7 of its zoning ordinance together with the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code. The Flood Zones page on the city's site describes each one.

  • Zone X sits outside the 0.2% annual chance flood area and is the least likely to flood.
  • Zone X shaded carries a 0.2% annual chance, and water stays under 1 foot in a 1% flood.
  • Zones AE, AH and AO face a 1% annual chance, and AE lists base flood elevations.
  • Zone VE is the velocity zone, where waves reach 3 feet or more.

Anyone can look up a property's zone and find elevation certificates on Forerunner, the city's public tool. A buyer will likely run the same search, so check your own address first and you will not be caught off guard.

sections.h2: Preparing for a buyer's flood questions
sections.html:
Before anyone tours the house, gather what a careful buyer will ask for: the flood zone result, any elevation certificate, and records of past water problems or insurance claims. Look at the crawl space, basement and lowest floor for water marks or a musty smell. If you fixed something, keep the receipt and any permit.

You do not have to repair a thing to sell. Knowing the answers simply lets you talk about the house with confidence and judge an offer fairly, whether it comes from a cash buyer or a family that needs a mortgage.

Military spending drives most of the local economy. Naval Station Norfolk hosts U.S. Fleet Forces Command as well as a NATO command. The Virginia Port Authority and Sentara Health are also headquartered in the city.

Orders can arrive with little warning, leaving a family a few weeks to move. A landlord with a short-lease tenant may likewise want to be out before the next rotation. Skipping the lender's approval process is what makes a cash sale workable on those timelines.

sections.h2: How Norfolk bills real estate tax
sections.html:
The City Assessor values your house, City Council chooses the rate, and the Treasurer collects what is owed, with payment four times a year on the dates above. The Treasurer bills more than 68,000 taxable parcels and mails the bills at least 30 days ahead.

For assessment questions, phone the City Assessor's Office at 757-664-4732. The Treasurer's Real Estate Tax page also gives tax relief contacts at the Department of Human Services.

Neighborhood Quality can send the Treasurer a nuisance abatement lien, which gives the owner 30 days to pay. Has the city ever mowed, hauled trash or dealt with a structure at your address? Get a payoff figure from the Treasurer before listing or signing.

Taxes left unpaid can end with the city auctioning the property under Virginia Code 58.1-3975. A sale on your own terms keeps the choice with you. Tax and liens are paid by the settlement agent out of your proceeds, so you do not have to find that money first.

sections.h2: Timing a Norfolk sale around the tax dates
sections.html: With bills due September 30, December 5, March 31 and June 5, a closing near one of those dates deserves a quick call to the Treasurer first. Ask which installment is current and whether your account shows anything unpaid. Whatever is owed at settlement comes out of your check, and the buyer's side will want proof that it was paid.

sections.h2: What does it take to sell a Norfolk house for cash?
sections.html:
A cash deal in Norfolk is governed by the same Virginia deed rules. It simply drops the buyer's loan and the inspection-driven repair list.

  • Collect your deed, newest tax bill and payoff letters.
  • Ask about city liens, nuisance abatement charges included.
  • Run your address through Forerunner for the flood zone.
  • Pick a settlement company, then sign the contract.

The state's grantor tax is 50 cents per $500 of value. Sellers ordinarily cover it, though a contract can say otherwise. Recording also requires the price on page one of the deed.

Both sides sign at the settlement company. From the price, the agent subtracts your mortgage payoff, city liens, unpaid tax and deed charges, then sends you what is left. Take photo ID, your loan account details and a copy of the deed if you have one, plus the lease when tenants live there.

With no lender in the picture, no appraisal gets ordered and the date seldom moves. Request exact figures from the settlement agent ahead of signing.

• Water damage in crawl spaces, basements and first floors on low lots.
  • Older houses with outdated wiring, plumbing or roofs.
  • Inherited houses with several heirs and no clear next step.
  • Rentals with tenants, deferred repairs or city notices.
  • Back taxes or city liens that must be paid at closing.

Each of these can drag out a listing, since buyers who need a loan tend to request repairs. Selling directly puts the closing date in your hands and lets the house go as it stands.

faqs.q: Is Norfolk a city or a county?
faqs.a: Norfolk is an independent city and sits inside no county. The city handles assessments, tax bills and zoning itself.

faqs.q: When are Norfolk real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: Bills come quarterly, due September 30, December 5, March 31 and June 5. The fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30.

faqs.q: How do I check whether my Norfolk house is in a flood zone?
faqs.a: Use Forerunner, the city's public lookup tool, linked from the Flood Zones page. It shows the zone, flood data and any elevation certificates on file for a property.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Norfolk house with unpaid city liens?
faqs.a: Yes. The liens are normally paid from your proceeds at closing. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff on any nuisance abatement charge and your settlement agent for the rest.

faqs.q: Who pays the Virginia grantor tax on a Norfolk sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays unless the contract has the buyer cover some or all of it. The rate is 50 cents for each $500 of value under Virginia Code 58.1-802.
